title: Feedback on table formatting
description:
Thank you for your continued work on many R tools, including `air`. I understand that you are open to feedback on the experimental table formatting, so I wanted to provide some comments.

For reference, here is the current table formatting from `air`, reproduced from [the docs](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/formatter.html#table-formatting).

```
tribble(
  ~customer   , ~product   , ~price  , ~units_sold ,
  "ACME"      , "Computer" , 1499.99 ,          25 ,
  "Globex"    , "Monitor"  ,  889.5  ,        1005 ,
  "Stark"     , "Tablet"   ,   99.99 ,         304 ,
  "WayneEnt." , "Tablet"   ,  259    ,          40 ,
)
```

Below are my reactions and opinions to the experimental feature, which I hope will be helpful, even if disregarded.

## Visually looks wrong and rules are unintuitive

My initial response and *opinion* is that this looks quite wrong. In fact, when I first saw it, I thought something in `air` was broken or that there was a weird conflict was happening with my Positron settings. The two main concerns that I see are (1) the rules are complex making it feel inconsistent and (2) there's an extra space introduced.

### Complex rules

Obviously, this is my opinion, but hopefully one based on experience: the complex rules look unformatted. When writing data in this way, I do not expect this set of alignment choices. In my own code, where I only had years (right-aligned) and strings (left-aligned) intermixed, rather than sorted it looked very weird because it bunches around the `,`s.

The core non-taste issue that I see is that depending on the content, it will refactor in as-if random ways, even if they are intended. Consider the case in which we add an explicit integer indicator to one of the entries. It produces:

```
tribble(
  ~customer   , ~product   , ~price  , ~units_sold ,
  "ACME"      , "Computer" , 1499.99 ,   25L       ,
  "Globex"    , "Monitor"  ,  889.5  , 1005        ,
  "Stark"     , "Tablet"   ,   99.99 ,  304        ,
  "WayneEnt." , "Tablet"   ,  259    ,   40        ,
)
```

or similarly, by being somewhat explicit as R would generally allow. This now converts to decimal-left aligned, even though the statements are equivalent. Why are some numeric statements right-aligned, but decimal numeric statements are left-aligned?

```
tribble(
  ~customer   , ~product   , ~price  , ~units_sold ,
  "ACME"      , "Computer" , 1499.99 ,   25        ,
  "Globex"    , "Monitor"  ,  889.5  , 1005.0      ,
  "Stark"     , "Tablet"   ,   99.99 ,  304        ,
  "WayneEnt." , "Tablet"   ,  259    ,   40        ,
)
```

These rules result in additional churn that looks like there's something wrong, rather than an intentional design. Yes, the integer will be converted, but this is how we might write the data if we are inputting mixed outputs, such as those from count models and linear models.

### Extra space

Even though some pieces are advertised as being right-aligned, there is always an extra space inserted. This isn't documented anywhere that I could find. I would expect it to look more like:

```
tribble(
  ~customer  , ~product  , ~price , ~units_sold,
  "ACME"     , "Computer", 1499.99,          25,
  "Globex"   , "Monitor" ,  889.5 ,        1005,
  "Stark"    , "Tablet"  ,   99.99,         304,
  "WayneEnt.", "Tablet"  ,  259   ,          40,
)
```

## What I would have expected

I understand the general desire for a table-based format. Flattening everything to `~col1,\n~col2...` makes it hard to edit, especially using Positron's format-on-save feature. In practice, I would expect something simple as a default styling. This avoids learning custom rules for specific functions.

Something like styler's format, which keeps correct line breaks but removes extra spaces:

```
tribble(
  ~customer, ~product, ~price, ~units_sold,
  "ACME", "Computer", 1499.99, 25,
  "Globex", "Monitor", 889.5, 1005,
  "Stark", "Tablet", 99.99, 304,
  "WayneEnt.", "Tablet", 259, 40,
)
```

Or, if leaning more into the table, something which logically and cleanly keeps columns in a consistent fashion. The below simply aligns the commas and the entries so you can see the columns in a predictable, logical way. This is robust to the decimal or `1L` type edits.

```
tribble(
    ~customer,   ~product,  ~price, ~units_sold,
       "ACME", "Computer", 1499.99,          25,
     "Globex",  "Monitor",   889.5,        1005,
      "Stark",   "Tablet",   99.99,         304,
  "WayneEnt.",   "Tablet",     259,          40,
)
```

Either of these are simple and logically formatted, without introducing complex rules. I can understand the idea behind the experimental feature, but it seems both unusual and very opinionated for a default, opt-out behavior.

Perhaps one consideration would be to have a default table formatting which is purposely simple: retain lines and remove spaces, like `styler` does and allow this choice to be a per-repo opt-in to get complex behavior.

title: `air format <file>.qmd` and `air format --stdin-file-path <file>.qmd` should maybe respect `default-include`
description:
We've seen a number of issues where people try `air format <file>.qmd` or `air format <file>.Rmd` and it either:
 
- Gives you an obscure parse error
- "Works" because by chance it parses, but totally breaks your qmd

This occurs because right now if you provide `air format <any-file>` then we just blindly assume you know what you are doing and try to format that file. That's mostly to support something like `air format NAMESPACE` or `air format r-text.txt` or `air format r-file-no-ext`.

I think we should reconsider this, and maybe force "directly supplied" files to also be subject to `default-include`, which today is just `"**/*.[R,r]"`, so it would limit Air to only being able to format R files at the command line. If we came across something that isn't "included", like `<file>.qmd`, then we'd either:

- Throw it out silently
- Throw it out with a warning, because the user clearly wanted to try and format this but we said no
- Totally error out, because the user clearly wanted to try and format this but we said no

The stdin case is even more ambiguous. We could:

- Reemit asis silently
- Reemit asis with a warning
- Totally error out

I would be in favor of switching to erroring out, as I think it would catch a lot of incorrect calls to air

I would also be in favor of not even providing a way to "force" air to format this non-R file, as I have never needed to do that and can't think of a compelling enough use case for it.

---

If we decide we can't do this, we should at least black list `.qmd` and `.rmd` when they are provided directly at the command line and error on those in particular.

title: `air format <file>.R` and `air format --stdin-file-path <file>.R` should respect `exclude` and `default-exclude`
description:
Extracted from https://github.com/posit-dev/air/pull/471

Currently if a user does

```bash
air format <file>.R
```

then `<file>.R` is unconditionally formatted, full stop, regardless of `exclude` and `default-exclude`.

This means that `air format renv/activate.R` would try to format `renv/activate.R`, even though it is part of `default-exclude` and should never be formatted. Similar results with any user provided `exclude`s.

I think this is wrong!

In particular, it makes it more difficult for tools such as pre-commit and RStudio to invoke air. Those tools have no way of knowing what `exclude`s or `default-exclude`s are, so when a user edits or saves `renv/activate.R`, both of them are very likely to just call:

```bash
air format renv/activate.R
```

This was a problem for ruff as well, so much so that they added a special `--force-exclude` option that they use in their default pre-commit hook:
https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit/blob/1629a02ed57c23345951c75547bfe5fb73970fd3/.pre-commit-hooks.yaml#L15

For them, `--force-exclude` means "Respect `exclude`s even for files provided directly on the command line".

I'd like to make the argument that we should just _always_ respect `exclude` and `default-exclude` for files provided directly on the command line.

It seems very unlikely that a user would really want to ever run `air format renv/activate.R`, but there is a real problem with the fact that pre-commit (and eventually RStudio when it uses stdin) do this right now and will change these files. So I'd advocate for the safer default.

title: Please sign air.exe to support institutional Windows environments
description:
In our institutional Windows 11 environment, executable files located in user space (e.g., under `C:\Users\...`) are blocked by default.

The Posit Air extension installs the following executable into user space:

```
C:\Users\<user>\.positron\extensions\posit.air-vscode-0.20.0\bundled\bin\air.exe
```

To allow it to run, our IT security policy requires the executable to be explicitly unblocked. Currently, this can only be done by file hash. This creates operational friction:

* Each time the extension updates, a new `air.exe` is installed.
* The hash changes with every release.
* The new executable must be manually re-approved.
* This disrupts workflows and requires repeated security exceptions.

At the moment, `air.exe` is not digitally signed.

In our environment, executables can alternatively be whitelisted based on a trusted code-signing certificate. If `air.exe` were digitally signed (e.g., by Posit Software, PBC), it could be approved once via publisher trust rather than per-version hash.

**Request**

Would it be possible to digitally sign `air.exe` in future releases of the extension?

This would significantly improve usability in enterprise and institutional environments with strict endpoint protection policies.

Thank you for considering this.

title: Possible `trailing-comma` option
description:
Consider the following tribble

```r
lookup <- tribble(
  ~from             , ~to               ,
  "UNC"             , "UNC Chapel Hill" ,
  "Chapel Hill"     , "UNC Chapel Hill" ,
  "Duke"            , "Duke"            ,
  "Duke University" , "Duke"
)
```

this would look nicer with a trailing comma

```r
lookup <- tribble(
  ~from             , ~to               ,
  "UNC"             , "UNC Chapel Hill" ,
  "Chapel Hill"     , "UNC Chapel Hill" ,
  "Duke"            , "Duke"            ,
  "Duke University" , "Duke"            ,
)
```

Similarly, it is commonly adopted in other languages to always add a trailing comma to expanded forms of constructs that allow them. Like in Rust

https://users.rust-lang.org/t/trailing-commas/13993/4

```rust
enum Message {
    Quit,
    Move { x: i32, y: i32 },
    Write(String),
    ChangeColor(i32, i32, i32), // <-- Trailing comma
}
```

The trailing comma here isn't required, but is considered good practice because _it makes refactoring easier_.

We have the same kind of idea in R with `list2()`, and anything that is built on it.

```r
list2(
  this,
  that,
  those, # <- trailing comma
)
```

`vec_c()` and other vctrs functions that take `...` are examples of something that is "built on" `list2()`:

```r
vctrs::vec_c(
  this,
  that,
  those,
)
```

It would be interesting to consider if we could have a means to support auto-adding trailing commas in expanded form for some cases like this.

If we went the route of doing something like `table` and `default-table`, then we could have:

- A default set of functions that would get trailing commas. Opt out of them with `default-trailing-comma: false`.
    - `list2()`
    - `tribble()`
    - dplyr verbs? `mutate()`? That would be generate a very noisy diff!

- A `trailing-comma = []` option where you can provide your own set of functions you'd like to prefer trailing commas in.

This would be a rather complex option because it would interact with `persistent-line-breaks`. For example:

```r
# Start with this
list2(this, that, those)

# Request expansion
list2(
this, that, those)

# Get this, note the new addition of the trailing comma as well
list2(
  this, 
  that, 
  those,
)

# Re-request flat
list2(this, 
  that, 
  those,
)

# ----
# Now what?

# Do we get this?
list2(this, that, those, )

# Do we refuse to flatten?

# Do we detect this was a trailing-comma function and remove it + flatten?
# That might be the best option, but is pretty complicated!
list2(this, that, those)
```

title: Single to multi-line formatting of assignment RHS
description:
Related: https://github.com/posit-dev/air/issues/183#issuecomment-2608175446
Related: https://github.com/posit-dev/air/issues/183#issuecomment-2608187667

The pipe operator (`|>`) and the assignment (`<-`) perform two different tasks: store into LHS and transition into RHS. I'd argue there should only be one task per piped line.

To me, the pipe operator's task is to `transition LHS into RHS` and can be repeated many times within an expression. It is fundamentally different from the assignment operator's task which is to `store RHS into LHS` and should only be performed once and causes a side effect of variable storage (`LHS`).

When glancing at multi-line code, I currently lose the assignment operator `<-` as it is lost in the middle of a line containing both an assignment and pipe operators:  `VARIABLE1 <- VARIABLE2 |>`. When scanning code quickly, it reads like a incorrectly formatted pipe expression.

Taking an example from https://github.com/posit-dev/air/issues/183#issuecomment-2608175446:

```
# before
foo <- this |> that() |> this_other_long_thing() |> and_this_one_too_as_well()

# current
foo <- this |>
  that() |>
  this_other_long_thing() |>
  and_this_one_too_as_well()
```

Ideally, I believe `this` should start on the next line.

```
# ideal
foo <-
  this |>
  that() |>
  this_other_long_thing() |>
  and_this_one_too_as_well()
```

And another example from https://github.com/posit-dev/air/issues/183#issuecomment-2608187667: (enhanced with numbers for each code block)

```
# 1. before
# If this
private$event_callback_counts[[domain]] <- my_special_function(with, really_really_really, long_arguments)
```
```
# 2.
# turned into this
private$event_callback_counts[[domain]] <- 
  my_special_function(with, really_really_really, long_arguments)
```
```
# 3.
# but then you typed more
private$event_callback_counts[[domain]] <- 
  my_special_function(with, really_really_really, long_arguments, long_arguments, long_arguments)
```
```
# 4.
# then it would respect the persistent line break and break as
private$event_callback_counts[[domain]] <- 
  my_special_function(
    with, 
    really_really_really, 
    long_arguments, 
    long_arguments, 
    long_arguments
  )
```
```
# 5.
# rather than what you'd really want, which is
private$event_callback_counts[[domain]] <- my_special_function(
  with, 
  really_really_really, 
  long_arguments, 
  long_arguments, 
  long_arguments
)
```

Classification:
1. (before)
2. Defendable as there is no `|>`, therefore it does not need to turn into # 4 prematurely.
3. (should always transition to # 4)
4. Ideal! No further changes to be made.
5. Current behavior. Not ideal. Use # 4 instead


----------------

Looking at more examples:

```
# before
asdfasdfasdfasdfsadf <- some_really_long_function_name(argument_one_very_long_name)
# current
asdfasdfasdfasdfsadf <- some_really_long_function_name(
  argument_one_very_long_name
)
# ideal; No need for multi
asdfasdfasdfasdfsadf <- 
  some_really_long_function_name(argument_one_very_long_name)
```

```
# With even more length
# before
asdfasdfasdfasdfsadf <-  some_really_long_function_name_asdfasdfasdf(argument_one_very_long_name)
# current
asdfasdfasdfasdfsadf <- some_really_long_function_name_asdfasdfasdf(
  argument_one_very_long_name_asdfasfd
```

title: Uneven Table Formatting when Using Umlauts
description:
Usually, air will pad table cells with spaces before commas to align them:

```R
foo <- tribble(
  ~egg , ~span     ,
  "1"  , "test"    ,
  "2"  , "teest"   ,
  "3"  , "teeeest" ,
  "4"  , "test"
)
```

When using umlauts (ß, ä, ü, ö, ...), the table cell containing the umlaut will get padded with a space less for each umlaut:

```R
foo <- tribble(
  ~egg , ~span     ,
  "1"  , "teßt"   ,
  "2"  , "test"    ,
  "3"  , "täst"   ,
  "4"  , "tääst" ,
  "5"  , "teeeest" ,
  "6"  , "test"
)
```

Interestingly, if I put more spaces than air can remove (it will keep one space before the comma of the cell containing the umlaut), air will increase the overall padding of that column:

```R
foo <- tribble(
  ~egg , ~span       ,
  "1"  , "teßt"     ,
  "2"  , "test"      ,
  "3"  , "täst"     ,
  "4"  , "tääst"   ,
  "5"  , "teeeest"   ,
  "6"  , "test"      ,
  "7"  , "täääst" ,
)
```

This happens with `air-0.8.0` using Zed. I haven't tested with other special characters yet, but probably some issue regarding characters vs UTF code points I'd guess? https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=dd8772ef90245d9c496435ebfdb690e1
If you need more information, please just ask.

```r
  a_really_long_symbol_name_that_requires_its_own_line_3 <- "hello, world"
```

`air` will format it like this

```r
    a_really_long_symbol_name_that_requires_its_own_line_3 <- "hello, world"
```

```r
  a_really_long_symbol_name_that_requires_its_own_line_3 <- "hello, world"
```

I used a simple example to illustrate the issue with just long symbol names, which is a pretty obscure use case. I've seen this in more practical examples when declaring multiple `S7` methods from the same function definition.

There's some precedence for this operator indentation, given how the `|>` is often used in `dplyr` chains.

title: Comment placement in argument lists causes ordering issues
description:
This call:

```r
list(
  # comment0
  foo  # comment1
  =1, bar  # comment2
  =  # comment3
  # comment4
  2 #comment5
  #comment6
  , #comment7
  #comment8
)
```

Is currently formatted as:

```r
list(
  # comment0
  # comment1
  foo = 1,
  # comment3
  # comment4
  # comment2
  bar = 2, #comment5 #comment7
  #comment8
  #comment6
)
```

We need to fix these issues:

- [ ] `comment2` is pulled down because it becomes a leading comment of the whole argument node
- [ ] `comment6` is pulled down because it becomes a leading comment of the empty argument, I think because it's an own-line and the default placement puts it on the next node.
- [ ] `comment7` is formatted on the same line as `comment5`, because they both become trailing comments of the same node, and both have `lines_before = 0`. This happens here: https://github.com/posit-dev/air/blob/e3655e9a68f18ba7caea0aa6680817553bc97bee/crates/air_r_formatter/src/comments.rs#L951

title: Release tags point to unreachable commits
description:
Steps to reproduce:

I was trying to package the air cli for Archlinux using a PKGBUILD file. 

This process has a convention to create a package named `air-git` to check out the latest code and build it.
It still needs a version number though, and a common way to achieve this is using `git describe` to find the latest annotated tag  (i.e. `x.z.y`) and add the count of commits since then and a commit hash (i.e. `x.y.z-n-h`). This allows for semver ordering.

I discovered that the `air` does not use annotated tags and I ran into this `git describe` behavior from `man git tag` 
 
> Annotated tags are meant for release while lightweight tags are meant for private or temporary object labels. For this reason, some git commands for naming objects (like git describe) will ignore lightweight tags by default.

Undeterred, I changed to using `git describe --tags` which also includes non-annotated tags, but that yields  `0.1.2-189-gd48bad1` far away from the current release `0.7.1`.  That is because the `0.7.1` tag (and other release tags) does not point to a commit that is part of any branch, which seem odd. See also the warning displayed at https://github.com/posit-dev/air/tree/0.7.1 

My expectation would have been for a release tag to point to a commit on `main` or at least to a commit on a release branch. It makes it a bit difficult otherwise to differentiate a rogue release from a regular one.

Is this behavior on purpose or is that something you'd be interested in changing (or rather, accept a PR for) so that I don't have to manually do a version bump ?

title: `prev_sibling()` and `next_sibling()` skip nodes of kind `L_PAREN` and `R_PAREN`
description:
It seems that `prev_sibling()` and `next_sibling()` (and potentially other functions) skip nodes of kind `L_PAREN` and `R_PAREN`. Is this expected?

### Example with `air_r_parser`

`foo.R`:
```r
(a)
``` 
The Air syntax tree shows this:

```
0: R_ROOT@0..4
  0: (empty)
  1: R_EXPRESSION_LIST@0..3
    0: R_PARENTHESIZED_EXPRESSION@0..3
      0: L_PAREN@0..1 "(" [] []
      1: R_IDENTIFIER@1..2
        0: IDENT@1..2 "a" [] []
      2: R_PAREN@2..3 ")" [] []
  2: EOF@3..4 "" [Newline("\n")] []
```

So I would expect that starting from the `R_IDENTIFIER` node and then taking the `prev_sibling()` returns the `L_PAREN` node, but it is not the case. With the following files, the previous sibling is `None`.

`main.rs`: 
```rust
use air_r_parser::RParserOptions;
use biome_rowan::AstNode;
use std::fs;

fn main() {
```

title: Consider upper and lower bounds on `line-width`
description:
In my own code, often I'd like to allow an 81-character line to stay on one line, for readability. Or I might split a 79-character line into two or three lines, for readability. Right now, air will force the former to multiple lines and the latter to one line.  Changing `line-width` can only fix one of these.

I would propose a configurable 'buffer zone' where the programmer's usage is stetted, i.e.:
- multilines which could fit under the lower bound are brought into a single line, but not multilines that would fit between the lower and upper bounds
- single lines longer than the upper bound are split into multilines, but not single lines shorter than the upper bound
I hope that's clear, 

Since `line-width` already exists, I'd propose something like `line-width-buffer` or `line-width-flex` or something, so that `line-width` would be the lower bound and `line-width` plus `line-width-flex` would be the upper bound.  Of course, by default, `line-width-flex: 0` so that the default behavior is not affected.

I understand the air team wants to keep things opinionated and non-configurable, but it's the lack of a little bit of flexibility that has held me back from using it everywhere.  This change would (I think) continue to minimize diffs from formatting changes, and would give programmers a bit more control of how to trade off horizontal and vertical space.

title: Consider adding "hugging" behavior for single argument functions with multi-line strings
description:
Both @jennybc and @hadley have reached out about how Air reformats code like this, which take advantage of the fact that both glue and cli will trim leading and trailing whitespace and newlines for you automatically

```r
# Jenny
glue::glue("
  To continue using the styler package, blah blah blah
")

# This results in this string, note no leading or trailing whitespace
# [1] "To continue using the styler package, blah blah blah"

# Hadley
r_agent$clone()$chat("
  This a 
  paragraph
  of 
  text
")
```

Air reformats to

```r
# Jenny
glue::glue(
  "
  To continue using the styler package, blah blah blah
"
)

# Hadley
r_agent$clone()$chat(
  "
  This a 
  paragraph
  of 
  text
"
)
```

This:
- Follows the conventional rule that "expands" the function fully
- Notably does not alter the whitespace _within_ the string in _any_ way. This is very important!

That said, you'd probably look at this and say "ew" and reformat like

```r
# Jenny
glue::glue(
  "To continue using the styler package, blah blah blah"
)

# Hadley
r_agent$clone()$chat(
  "This a 
  paragraph
  of 
  text"
)
```

Here you've manually tweaked the actual whitespace in the string (something Air won't do), even though the end result is the same due to how glue / cli trim outer whitespace.

The glue example looks fine like this, but the chat example feels like a noticeable loss in readability compared to where we originally started.

@jennybc has also noted that even though the glue example looks fine after the manual tweak, she will often write glue strings in this form...

```r
glue::glue("
  To continue using the styler package, blah blah blah
")
```

...with the assumption that one day she may come back and make this string multiline and more complicated, and can do so with a minimal diff / amount of mental effort.

---

So, given all this, we could start to think about a rule where:

- For function calls (and `[` and `[[` calls, which we treat functionally the same)
- With exactly 1 argument
- And the argument has no comments attached to it
- And the argument is a string (but probably not a raw string?)
- And the string itself is multiline (which I think we can detect, also watch out for our string line ending normalization routines)
- And there is no leading line break before the string

Then we perform a "hug" between the `("` and the `")`

The notable thing about the hug is that it does not affect whitespace _within_ the string itself, avoiding any potential invalidation of string contents. It only affects whitespace between the `(` and `"` and `"` and `)`, i.e. outside the string contents.

Here are a number of potential test cases

```r
# stays as is
fn("
  this
")

# stays as is
fn("
  this
  is
  a
  paragraph
")

# stays as is
fn("this
")

# stays as is
fn("
this")

# notably stays as is - leading persistent line break
fn(
  "this"
)

# from
fn(
  "this")
# to
fn(
  "this"
)

# from
fn("
  this
  that"
)
# to
fn("
  this
  that")

# stays as is
fn(
  # comment
  "
  this
  "
)

# uncertain, depends on comment placement rules
fn("
  this
" # comment
)

# uncertain, depends on comment placement rules
fn("
  this
"
# comment
)
```

title: Consider limiting format directive comments to own-line comments
description:
TLDR is that I think we should respect

```r
# fmt: skip
fn(
 a, b
)
```

but ignore (and possibly lint)

```r
fn(
 a, b # fmt: skip
)
```

I have many feelings about this, but the overarching rationale is that it is _very_ hard to have precise semantic meaning with end-of-line comments, and it is much easier to have precise semantic meaning with own-line comments that _lead a node_.

This would be much more similar to how rustfmt works, because their skip attribute is _node based_. They simply cannot have end-of-line attributes, so they don't have to think about this at all.

```rust
#[rustfmt::skip]
fn()
```

---

There is a very very good summary of this on the ruff side, where they have basically come to the same conclusion
https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/discussions/6670

In particular, https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/discussions/6670#discussioncomment-6788116

> are there any lessons we should takeaway for any suppression comment redesigns we explore in the future?

> Don't use trailing end-of-line comments. I don't have too strong evidence because I haven't looked as much into the other comments, but they seem the hardest to preserve. My impression (and prettier's recommendation) is to use leading own line comments, ideally, such that are node-based (they suppress the next node and not the next line).

--- 

Here is Prettier's advice:

https://prettier.io/docs/next/rationale#comments

> Generally, you get the best results when placing comments on their own lines, instead of at the end of lines. Prefer // eslint-disable-next-line over // eslint-disable-line.

---

I think we should strongly consider the possibility of limiting our "magic" comments to own-line only, and try and make them as "node based" as possible, as this is likely going to make our lives a lot easier, and behavior more predicable for users.

title: if/else formatting can lead to unexpected breaks
Clarify `switch()` formatting and then sync it with tidyverse style guide
description:
Hi

I have two questions regarding the formatting of `switch()` statements.

The first is: according to the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#switch-statements) we put `EXPR` directly after the opening bracket, i.e., on the same line. As long as we are within the preferred/configured maximum line length, `line-width`, of course. For example like in {tidyr}'s unnest-auto.R https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/1c970848703293049a6c7af0b63afb4d4f2c8e6f/R/unnest-auto.R#L28 before AIR formatting

```
switch(dir,
  longer = unnest_longer(data, {{ col }}, indices_include = FALSE),
  longer_idx = unnest_longer(data, {{ col }}, indices_include = TRUE),
  wider = unnest_wider(data, {{ col }}, names_repair = "unique")
)
```

Or the current example in the style guide (again: https://style.tidyverse.org/syntax.html#switch-statements)

```
switch(x,
  a = ,
  b = 1,
  c = 2,
  stop("Unknown `x`", call. = FALSE)
)
```

AIR puts `EXPR` on a new line, i.e., at the same indentation level as the listed arguments. E.g.

```
switch(
  dir,
  longer = unnest_longer(data, {{ col }}, indices_include = FALSE),
  longer_idx = unnest_longer(data, {{ col }}, indices_include = TRUE),
  wider = unnest_wider(data, {{ col }}, names_repair = "unique")
)
```

The second question concerns short `switch()` calls. What AIR does is correct, both according to the style guide and the AIR docs. This is "Each element should go on its own line unless all element_s_ can fit on one line.". I just thought let's raise the question now, i.e., not too late in developement, whether we like it or whether we think having multiline formatting is easier to read, even if it would fit on one line.

```
switch(x, a = , b = 1, c = 2, stop("Unknown `x`", call. = FALSE))
```

On both questions, I am interested in hearing thoughts on this from the tidyverse team, both what is technically possible with AIR and what we as developers prefer.

Side note: that we typically prefer `rlang::abort()`/`cli::cli_abort()` instead of `stop()` is not relevant for the question here.

title: Multiline anonymous functions should forcibly have their `body` wrapped in `{ }`
description:
```r
\(x) if (is.na(x)) "CRAN" else cli::cli_fmt(cli::cli_text("{.field {x}} field in DESCRIPTION"))
```

Currently formatted as

```r
\(x)
  if (is.na(x)) "CRAN" else
    cli::cli_fmt(cli::cli_text("{.field {x}} field in DESCRIPTION"))
```

I think in this case it should really be:

```r
\(x) {
  if (is.na(x)) {
    "CRAN"
  } else {
    cli::cli_fmt(cli::cli_text("{.field {x}} field in DESCRIPTION"))
  }
}
```

i.e. if a user requested line break is already there before the body, or the whole thing can't fit on one line, then forcibly add `{ }`. Because as soon as you add a second statement, you need them anyways.

title: Consider a global fallback `air.toml` location
description:
Right now, if we can't find an `air.toml` as we walk up the directory tree, then we give up and use the "default" settings of `Settings::default()`.

Ruff has support for also considering a user specified default configuration in this case, instead of `Settings::default()`:
https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/#config-file-discovery

> If no config file is found in the filesystem hierarchy, Ruff will fall back to using a default configuration. If a user-specific configuration file exists at ${config_dir}/ruff/pyproject.toml, that file will be used instead of the default configuration, with ${config_dir} being determined via [etcetera's native strategy](https://docs.rs/etcetera/latest/etcetera/#native-strategy), and all relative paths being again resolved relative to the current working directory.

I'm not 100% convinced we should spend time on this yet, but in #308 there is a reasonable case for wanting this so that all users / projects on an RStudio Server instance would get the same formatting out of the box.

Technically if you place an `air.toml` at root level `~/`, then I think we will find it for any project that doesn't have a "closer" `air.toml`, but that feels fairly unofficial and a little sketchy compared to a feature like this.

---

The usage of etcetera is nice because the locations it looks for config files in are platform specific, and also respect env vars that end users can set before launching Air (it uses the XDG specification on Unix, and USERPROFILE on Windows)

title: Use custom cargo-dist binary building workflows
description:
In https://github.com/posit-dev/air/pull/301 we had to pin ourselves to Rust 1.83 due to the aarch64-pc-windows-msvc build and cargo-xwin.

cargo-xwin's docker contain pulls in 1.83 by default, and while that is configurable, it is not available to us to change. See the PR above for full info.

To free us to use Rust 1.84+, and to give us more control over the binary building process of cargo-dist in general, we should look into setting

```
# Whether CI should include auto-generated code to build local artifacts
build-local-artifacts = false
# Local artifacts jobs to run in CI
local-artifacts-jobs = ["./build-binaries"]
```

Where `build-binaries.yml` is our own workflow that builds binaries for all platforms of interest. For each target, we would be in charge of:
- Building the binary and wrapping it into a `tar.gz` (Unix) or `zip` (Windows)
- Computing the SHA
- Uploading both as GitHub artifacts

If we do both of those, cargo-dist should be able to pick up from there and generate the GitHub Release and the installer scripts, both of which are still very valuable parts of the cargo-dist process.

Ruff has done this. While they use maturin, I don't think we should let that deter us from looking at their approach (under the hood, maturin uses cargo-xwin and cargo-zigbuild, so at some point it's similar to what we'd manually do):
https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/main/.github/workflows/build-binaries.yml

It's going to take some effort to get the CI set up correctly for all targets (cross compilation for ARM Windows, cargo-zigbuild usage or PyPa docker containers for old Linux support), but ultimately having more full over the build process is probably going to be good in the long run due to cargo-dist having no maintainer right now, and because the build process has been a source of frustration for us over the months.

title: Review incorrect VS Code extension activation events
description:
With my newly acquired knowledge of glob syntax, I can say that `workspaceContains:*.R` and `workspaceContains:*.r` represent "any R file at the workspace root". This is not what we were going for, we wanted Air to be started if there were any R files in any directory under the workspace root. That would have been `workspaceContains:**/*.R`. You can confirm that Air doesn't immediately start up by opening a project with R files in a subfolder (and no editors open) and looking for `Air Language Server` in the Output pane. It won't be there.

I'm not actually sure we should use `**/*.R` though. This comment notes that it can be expensive in large projects https://github.com/sourcery-ai/sourcery/issues/112 (that comment also confirms my beliefs about how this glob syntax works).

In monorepos like Arrow, that could be _super_ slow, and they also probably don't want Air active when they are working on, say, C++ things.

Instead I think we should be like the vscode-python extension (https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-python/blob/6b7d8d1c12189126dce4c5d6733a74ab7762fb00/package.json#L71) and look for certain files at the workspace root that would be a good signal to preemptively activate on. I'm thinking:
- `air.toml`
- `.air.toml`
- `DESCRIPTION` (good for packages and projects that use this file)
- maybe something renv related? 

We would still keep `"onLanguage:r"` so that if any R file is opened the extension boots up, but this would allow it to preemptively start up in R packages and in any repo with `air.toml` at the workspace root.

description:
See https://github.com/r-lib/usethis/pull/2109#issuecomment-2695466329


The current initial workflow for Air in Positron for an _existing_ project looks like:
- Install Air CLI
- Install Air OpenVSX Extension
- `usethis::use_air()`
- Commit
- `air format .` one time using the Air CLI to get the whole project in order
- Commit
- Switch to Format on Save using the Air Extension from here on out

The current initial workflow for Air in RStudio for an _existing_ project looks like:
- Install Air CLI
- `usethis::use_air()`
- Commit
- `air format .` one time using the Air CLI to get the whole project in order
- Commit
- Switch to Format on Save using Air as an "external formatter" from here on out

I don't think we can improve on RStudio any further unless it bundles Air. But with VS Code / Positron I'd like to remove the CLI from the picture so it looks like:
- Install Air OpenVSX Extension
- `usethis::use_air()`
- Commit
- Run `Air: Format project` using the Air Extension
- Commit
- Switch to Format on Save using the Air Extension from here on out

I don't think having `use_air()` try and invoke Air will be super helpful here, as it will have a pre-req that Air is installed as a command line tool, and in our ideal world that actually won't be the case for Positron users (it'll be bundled in the extension but not available at the command line unless they install it themselves)


---

(This is an idea that @lionel- and I have talked about a little before, this is just a concrete writeup)

I think `Air: Format project` will be a little tricky because it is not natively part of the LSP and probably never will be. I think there are some issues in upstream VS Code requesting this feature that have been there for years. A few thoughts on it:

- It will likely be VS Code and Positron specific
- It probably will not go through the LSP? We essentially would have to perform `did_open`, `format`, `did_close` on every single discovered document that we need to format.
- We probably want to make sure every R editor is saved and closed before performing the format.
    - Ensuring the editors are closed should help the LSP stay in sync after the project wide formatting occurs. It'll just get a new did-open notification next time the user opens an R file with the refreshed contents.
- We probably want to refuse to format if there are any unstaged Git changes
- We can likely move `air format .` infra to a more generic place and reuse bits of that (but see adjacent idea below)
- It would likely require an `air.toml` to exist in the project so that we don't have to worry about forward propagation of editor specific settings (the `air.toml`s presence overrides forward propagation). That makes it nicely aligned with the `air format .` behavior.
- I'm not sure how we'd report errors about failures in individual files.

Possible adjacent idea:
- What if `Air: Format project` has all the restrictions from above but just literally opens a new VS Code Terminal and runs `air format .` in there? We know the path to the bundled binary, so we can run `format` using that even though the user doesn't typically have access to it from their own command line (because its not on the PATH). That might be pretty nice actually cause it would also report errors, and doesn't require any refactoring on our end.

title: Zed: Issue with setting `logLevel`
description:
If you set

```json
    "air": {
      "initialization_options": {
        "logLevel": "trace"
      }
    }
```

Then it correctly sets the log level to `"trace"` using the initialization option of `air.logLevel`, but if you change anything in the configuration after that then we try and re-pull the non-initialization version of `air.logLevel` (as we refresh everything) but this time around `air.logLevel` is `None`, so we end up reverting the log level back to `"info"`, throwing out that initialization option of `"trace"`.

This isn't a problem in VS Code because `air.logLevel` corresponds to both what we pull as the initialization option AND what we pull dynamically. In Zed I think they are separate, although I can't figure out how to set the non-initialization option of `air.logLevel` (it might not be possible).

We could say "if we pull `air.logLevel=None` and we have a previously set `logLevel`, then don't update the log level", but I worry about what that would mean for vs code, because in VS Code you may start with

```
"air.logLevel": "trace"
```

but then you may remove that line and expect it to go back to `"info"`, but it won't if we do this. Although that may be a small price to pay for it to work mostly as expected elsewhere.

``` R

# fmt: skip

```

Perhaps something like `# fmt: align-assign` could align assignments on consecutive lines, e.g:

``` R
# fmt: align-assign
my_var       <- 123

my_unaligned_var <- 456

```

title: Wrapping at infix operator in long if statement chain

description:
For:

- `switch()`
- R6, S7, ggproto (e.g. https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2/blob/main/R/coord-map.R#L156)

I.e. functions that have one or more leading setup arguments followed by a list of key-values. A common style for these is to write the leading arguments on the same line and only expand the list of key-values.

```r
switch(foo,
  a = 1,
  b = 2
)
```

Air currently fully expands:

```r
switch(
  foo,
  a = 1,
  b = 2
)
```

We could:

- Special-case `switch()`
- Add an air.toml section with a list of functions and the number of sticky argument

Using the array-of-objects syntax for toml:

```toml
[format]

[[format.sticky]]
name = "ggproto"
n = 2

# Undo the default special-case for `switch()`
[[format.sticky]]
name = "switch"
number = 0
```

The fully expanded style could still be opted-into via a persistent line.

title: Enable Link-Time Optimization (LTO) and codegen-units = 1
description:
Hi!

I noticed that in the `Cargo.toml` file Link-Time Optimization (LTO) for the project is not enabled. I suggest switching it on since it will reduce the binary size (always a good thing to have) and will likely improve the application's performance. If you want to read more about LTO and its possible modes, I recommend starting from [this](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/codegen-options/index.html#lto) Rustc documentation.

I think you can enable LTO only for the Release builds so as not to sacrifice the developers' experience while working on the project, since LTO consumes an additional amount of time to finish the compilation routine. In this case, we can create a dedicated `[profile.optimized-dev]` profile where LTO will be disabled (so developers experience will not be affected). If we enable it on the Cargo profile level for the Release profile, users, who install the application with `cargo install`, will get the LTO-optimized version of the app "automatically". E.g., check `cargo-outdated` Release [profile](https://github.com/kbknapp/cargo-outdated/blob/master/Cargo.toml#L48). You also could be interested in other optimization options like `codegen-units = 1` - it also brings improvements over the current defaults.

Basically, it can be enabled with the following lines:

```
[profile.release]
codegen-units = 1
lto = true
```
If we enable it for the Release profile, according to the current scripts it will automatically be applied to the Dist profile as well.

I have made quick tests (AMD Ryzen 5900x, Fedora 41, Rust 1.84.1, the latest version of the project at the moment, `cargo build --profile dist --workspace` command) - here are the results:

* Dist (current default): 12 MiB, clean build time: 59s (UPD: the right clean build time is about 35s)
* Dist + `codegen-units = 1` + Fat LTO: 8 MiB, clean build time: 70s

Thank you.

title: Versioning of the Air Code extension
description:
VS Code recommends a super weird versioning strategy if you plan to have release and pre-release versions of your extension
https://code.visualstudio.com/api/working-with-extensions/publishing-extension#prerelease-extensions

> We only support major.minor.patch for extension versions, semver pre-release tags are not supported. Versions must be different between pre-release and regular releases. That is, if 1.2.3 is uploaded as a pre-release, the next regular release must be uploaded with a distinct version, such as 1.2.4. Full semver support will be available in the future.

> VS Code will automatically update extensions to the highest version available, so even if a user opted-into a pre-release version and there is an extension release with a higher version, the user will be updated to the released version. So, we recommend that extensions use major.EVEN_NUMBER.patch for release versions and major.ODD_NUMBER.patch for pre-release versions. For example: 0.2.* for release and 0.3.* for pre-release.

> If extension authors do not want their pre-release users to be updated to the release version, we recommend always incrementing and publishing a new pre-release version before publishing a release version to make sure that the pre-release version is always higher. Note that while pre-release users will be updated to a release version if it is higher, they still remain eligible to automatically update to future pre-releases with higher version numbers than the release version.

---

I think we may consider using a pre-release version if we want to send out an experimental feature? I doubt we'd set up nightly releases because that's probably too easy to break.

Ruff uses a calendar-ish based versioning scheme that seems reasonable:

- We'd start with `2025.0.0` and every _release_ we bump to the next _even_ minor version, so `2025.2.0`
- Every year we bump the major version, so `2026.0.0` at the start of next year
- We don't use the patch version at all and just keep it `0` (unless we really need it)

title: Consider treating `.Rproj` as a "virtual" `air.toml`
description:
With @lionel-:

During TOML discovery, we could also consider looking for `.Rproj` files "for historical reasons".

We'd treat `.Rproj` as nearly at the same level as `air.toml` in terms of importance, like:

air.toml > .Rproj > editor settings > air defaults

If we don't detect an `air.toml`, but do detect an `.Rproj`, then we would not consider any other settings, even if we were in VS Code / Positron. It would be like having an air.toml which overrides everything else to help enforce project level settings that everyone is forced to use.

An `.Rproj` looks like this, with `UseSpacesForTab` and `NumSpacesForTab` being the most important that we'd be looking for. We'd translate those into an in memory virtual `air.toml` and use that virtual toml file.

```
Version: 1.0
ProjectId: ad2d6033-a5dd-4de0-8c51-ed8a768f5b37

RestoreWorkspace: Default
SaveWorkspace: Default
AlwaysSaveHistory: Default

EnableCodeIndexing: Yes
UseSpacesForTab: Yes
NumSpacesForTab: 2
Encoding: UTF-8

RnwWeave: Sweave
LaTeX: pdfLaTeX

AutoAppendNewline: Yes
StripTrailingWhitespace: Yes
```

This would be nice for people that only work in RStudio because the workflow would be like:
- Update RStudio UI, which changes the on disk `.Rproj`
- Just rerun `air format` at the CLI over all files in the directory or save a file where `Format on Save` is active

Since air is treated as a CLI tool in RStudio, there is no syncing that needs to occur, it would just rediscover that updated `.Rproj` before the next format request.

---

The upside is that it means the settings RStudio uses for automatic indentation are in sync with what air tries to format your code to without extra effort.

The downside is that it would be one more level of potential confusion. And if you transition to Positron from RStudio you might be confused about why (kind of hidden) RStudio settings are being preferred over your editor settings.

An alternative is to have an easy way to create an `air.toml` from an `.Rproj`, but this won't have the nice property of staying in sync with the RStudio UI.

title: Propagate air.toml settings to Code and Positron
description:
See #133 for more context.

With #148 we now propagate client-side settings to Air to use as defaults for files that are not governed by an air.toml file. But we also need the opposite propagation: if there is an air.toml file, the client should reflect and respect the hard-coded settings. The rulers should be set accordingly, indentation should use the appropriate indentation style and width, etc.

This problem is similar to what the editorconfig extension does with editorconfig files: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=EditorConfig.EditorConfig.

> This plugin attempts to override user/workspace settings with settings found in .editorconfig files. No additional or vscode-specific files are required. As with any EditorConfig plugin, if root=true is not specified, EditorConfig will continue to look for an .editorconfig file outside of the project.

This seems like a nice behaviour we could implement for air.toml files.

I'm imagining it will work with a new custom LSP request from the client to the server to query the current air.toml configuration for a path in the form of LSP settings. This way we don't have to parse/resolve the air.toml files in the client.

title: Turning client-side settings into air.toml files
description:
With #148 we now support client-side settings. As mentioned by @jennybc, it would be helpful to provide a way to turn such settings into an air.toml file. I'm imagining a custom LSP request that takes a folder path and produces the side effect of creating an air.toml file based on client settings.

- The client sends the request to the server with the path. It should be a folder.
- We send a `configuration` request from the server to the client with all relevant settings, for that path.
- We get the results and use these to create an air.toml file in the folder.

This can be exposed as a Code command.

And the nice thing is that it would be a convenient way of snapshotting client-side settings in extension tests (cc @juliasilge). We'd set up different scenarios of settings and ask the LSP to create a snapshot of those settings in the form of an air.toml file.

This could also be a way to support editorconfig on the client side (cc @jmcphers). Users of editorconfig files probably have the editorconfig extension enabled, which means the workspace is automatically set up to use the editorconfig settings. So the request described above would be a way to transform an editorconfig file into an air.toml one, at least from VS Code and Positron. Edit: Actually not really because editorconfig changes the settings of _editors_, not the settings of _workspaces_, which we would really need here.

title: Design for formatting options
description:
We have two competing goals:

- Consistency of formatting _across_ IDEs. It should not matter whether you are using Positron, vim, or VS Code. The formatter should produce the same output. The main way to ensure this consistency is the air.toml configuration file.

- Consistent of formatting _within_ IDEs. Indentation should be consistent with formatting. IDE-specific settings for formatting (indent style, width, etc) should be taken into account in the absence of an air.toml file.

Configuration of indentation is a complex landscape:

- We want our own air.toml config file
- IDEs have user/global settings (sometimes language-specific)
- There are IDE-specific config files for a project such as Rproj and VS Code workspace settings
- There are cross-IDEs config files such as `editorconfig` (https://editorconfig.org/)

The CLI is a tool that is independent of IDEs. The only way to configure it is via air.toml. However the LSP also needs to care about IDE settings.


### IDE settings

The IDE can communicate settings via:

- Settings watched by the server and communicated by the client via the `didChangeConfiguration` LSP notification. The indentation configuration can be requested for each document of interest, which allows the client to resolve global/language/project settings. For the purpose of the server, this is just "user configuration".

- The `DocumentFormattingOptions` passed as argument to formatting requests. In the case of VS Code / Positron, this is the most accurate / up-to-date way of getting formatting settings. Unfortunately, changing the specific indentation settings of an editor (e.g. via the status bar or command palette) doesn't trigger a `didChangeConfiguration` notification.

  Although this should be the preferred way of ingesting formatting settings, watching the client's configuration is also important because some formatting tasks will not be initiated by a format request but by an assist or other refactoring tasks which might not pass formatting options.

  When we get a formatting request that does have formatting options, we should treat it as a notification and update settings for the document. This way further formatting operations such as described in the previous paragraph will have up-to-date settings if a VS Code / Positron user changed editor settings.


### editorconfig and the like

In the LSP we probably don't want to deal with things like editorconfig and instead let IDEs handle these, e.g. via https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=EditorConfig.EditorConfig. We can treat these settings as "IDE settings".

For the CLI it might be nice to handle editorconfig in some way. We could provide a tool to generate an air.toml file from an editorconfig file. This would simplify things internally.


### air.toml support in IDEs

Up to now we've discussed how Air should respect IDE settings for formatting in the absence of an air.toml file. But we also need to think about the opposite: how can IDE respect Air settings in the presence of an air.toml file?

IDEs do not always consult the LSP for formatting tasks. For instance, VS Code and Positron have internal rules to do indentation. We can implement format-as-you-type for `\n` but the LSP response comes noticeably later, causing a noticeable indentation change. So it's still desirable to keep the indentation settings in sync. In general there are other actions for which the LSP is never consulted, such as moving lines up or down.

To achieve intra-IDE consistency for indentation, the IDE should be sensitive to the configuration in air.toml. This is the job of IDE extensions. Should they provide a command to update workspace settings from the air.toml file? Should they detect mismatches and let the user know via notification?


### Summary

In general we want to respect this order of precedence in the LSP:

```
air.toml > IDE settings > Default Air settings
```

And the CLI is simply:

```
air.toml > Default Air settings
```

This way we should be able to keep the complexity of formatting configuration to a manageable level.

title: Can we have one "source of truth" for all air options?
description:
Follow up to https://github.com/posit-dev/air/pull/122

Here are the current set of options:

- `IndentStyle`
- `IndentWidth`
- `LineEnding` (note, `Auto` option in TOML file)
- `LineLength`
- `MagicLineBreak` (note, boolean in TOML file)

Right now we are kind of in a weird place. We have our own shim types for the options that come from Biome because we want to add extra features or have different defaults. But if we change the defaults of these shim types in the `workspace` crate, that isn't reflected in our tests in `air_r_formatter`.

This makes me think we should explore having a single "source of truth" for each of these options.

I'm thinking that `air_r_formatter` should be the home for all of these options shims. Our `RFormatOptions` struct would use _our_ option types, and our implementation of biome's `FormatOptions` trait (like `indent_style() -> IndentStyle`) is where we'd convert to the Biome type for use within the guts of the formatter.

We'd go ahead and add serde capabilities here, for use in the workspace crate.

This would allow us to make `air_r_formatter` the source of truth for these options, and if we change the default there it propagates out everywhere (including tests).

The one exception would be `LineEnding`, since in the TOML file we support an additional `Auto` option that the formatter doesn't actually see (the formatter gets the resolved result of the auto option). We'd have 2 copies of `LineEnding`, one without `Auto` in `air_r_formatter`, and one with `Auto` in the workspace crate. This would be the way we'd handle any other options going forward that need a slightly different representation for use in the TOML file.

title: Tabular formatting
description:
A comment like `# fmt: tabular` would instruct Air to format the next expression (which should be a function call) with these rules:

- The first line of arguments determines the number of columns
- The remaining arguments are wrapped according to the number of columns
- Arguments are aligned at commas

Difficulties:

- Investigate how to hook into Biome's infra to add this special formatting

title: Normalize line endings in multiline strings
description:
See also https://github.com/posit-dev/air/pull/69#issuecomment-2502473548

We have this CI failures on Windows https://github.com/posit-dev/air/actions/runs/12042018483/job/33574939950?pr=69

With this test

```
---- formatter::r::specs::r::value::string_value_r stdout ----
thread 'formatter::r::specs::r::value::string_value_r' panicked at C:\Users\runneradmin\.cargo\git\checkouts\biome-d49ce8898b420a50\2648fa4\crates\biome_formatter\src\builders.rs:394:5:
The content 'r"("some raw string
business")"' contains an unsupported '\r' line terminator character but text must only use line feeds '\n' as line separator. Use '\n' instead of '\r' and '\r\n' to insert a line break in strings.
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

Which formats a file containing this string

```r
r"("some raw string
business")"
```

Note that this is a _multiline string_. The raw string there isn't critical to the reprex, it's just what we happened to have there.

This fails because:
- On windows, git checks the file out with CRLF line endings. Note this puts a `\r\n` inside the string contents.
- The formatter fails inside `located_token_text()` for a string because of this [no-\r assertion](https://github.com/biomejs/biome/blob/cd1c8ec4249e8df8d221393586d664537c9fddb2/crates/biome_formatter/src/builders.rs#L365)

Both biome and ruff use this assertion, so I imagine it is for a good reason.

The way both of them handle this is by using variants of `normalize_string()` here:
https://github.com/biomejs/biome/blob/cd1c8ec4249e8df8d221393586d664537c9fddb2/crates/biome_formatter/src/token/string.rs#L48

Note that the docs say one of the things it does is replace `\r\n` with just `\n`.

They call this at `fmt()` time for a string node, before it actually drops through to `located_token_text()`, so they get a chance to "fix up" the string here. We could probably create our own version of this and strip out everything except the `\r\n` conversion, until we decide to do more normalization.


## Why do they even do this?

I imagine the idea is that typically the line ending doesn't really matter, it becomes part of the Trivia set, but is not part of an actual node. But here, the line ending gets parsed into the actual string contents. I assume they want to ensure that the actual nodes of the tree look the same across OSes regardless of line endings, and standardizing on `\n` inside multiline strings is the way to achieve that.

description:
Ruff has this beautifully simple algorithm for sending back 1 minimal-ish `TextEdit` during document format

- Usage https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/blob/24c90d6953a127c79f0b2cca17093249864f3f78/crates/ruff_server/src/server/api/requests/format.rs#L127-L141

In the 99% case when the user is actively typing and resaving, the `TextEdit` is very tightly scoped to a small part of the file, so we dont need to "edit" the whole file every time.

The way `between()` effectively works is that it finds the `first byte` between `source` and `modified` that has changed, and then it iterates in reverse and finds the `first byte from the end` that has changed. That becomes the range of the text edit to send back, which is typically much smaller!

title: Can we put some operators at the beginning of lines?
description:
There is a very popular issue in prettier about putting the operators of multiline binary expressions at the beginning of lines
https://github.com/prettier/prettier/issues/3806

Lots of languages do prefer operators at the beginning, as it improves readability:
https://github.com/prettier/prettier/issues/3806#issuecomment-1649159560

It also has the same benefits of trailing commas, you can often rearrange multiline conditions with a simple copy paste if the operator is leading:

```r
# Start here
this_thing
  && that_thing
  && this_other_thing

# Decide this_other_thing should go second, simple copy paste of the whole line
this_thing
  && this_other_thing
  && that_thing

# Compared to
this_thing && 
  that_thing && 
  this_other_thing

# Changing to this, which is not a simple copy paste of full lines
this_thing && 
  this_other_thing && 
  that_thing
```

I tend to agree with the readability argument (the trailing comma argument is less convincing to me), the pep style guide has a good motivating example:
https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#should-a-line-break-before-or-after-a-binary-operator

```python
# Wrong:
# operators sit far away from their operands
income = (gross_wages +
          taxable_interest +
          (dividends - qualified_dividends) -
          ira_deduction -
          student_loan_interest)

# Correct:
# easy to match operators with operands
income = (gross_wages
          + taxable_interest
          + (dividends - qualified_dividends)
          - ira_deduction
          - student_loan_interest)
```

This might be a bit tricky for R code (and maybe for Python?) because at top level or inside `{` this is invalid R code without being wrapped in `()` (like in the Python example):

```r
# Invalid R code at top level
income <- gross_wages
          + taxable_interest
          + (dividends - qualified_dividends)
          - ira_deduction
          - student_loan_interest

# This works
income <- (gross_wages
          + taxable_interest
          + (dividends - qualified_dividends)
          - ira_deduction
          - student_loan_interest)
```

It's somewhat common to see this kind of thing in if statements (though I'd argue you should create a simpler `condition`...)

```r
if (
  this_thing
    && that_thing
    && this_other_thing
) {
  body
}
```

We'd also have to consider pipelines, which are also sequences of binary operators. It's mostly easy with `%>%` and `|>`, they just never split this way. But with `+`? That's tricky because it could be a ggplot2 sequence or just a sequence of arithmetic operations!

```r
# `+` is always trailing here, not leading.
ggplot(data) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_bar()
```

title: Respecting empty lines and line breaks
description:
In 99% of air, the main idea is to strip out all existing formatting and reapply "the one true way" that is defined by air. There are a few places where we want to make an exception to this, which roughly fall into two categories:
- User requested empty lines
- User requested line breaks 

# Empty lines

## Empty lines between top level expressions

Rather than formatting these:

```r
1 + 1

2 + 2
```

as

```r
1 + 1
2 + 2
```

we respect exactly 1 empty line between expressions. In other words, if there are >1 lines

```r
1 + 1


2 + 2
```

then it gets reduced to

```r
1 + 1

2 + 2
```

## Empty lines between call arguments

For the same reason as top level expressions we retain the empty line between `x` and `y` here

```r
fn(
  x = function() {
    y
  }

  # This is a really important argument that deserves its own comment, the empty line above this is retained
  y = function() {
    y
  }
)
```

This is quite common in Shiny world and in R6, where arguments are complex functions and often you do separate them with a full empty line, often with a comment as well (or some roxygen docs in the R6 case)

# Line breaks

## Line breaks between call arguments

Consider the following list

```r
x <- list(
  foo = 1,
  bar = 2,
  baz = "three"
)
```

this totally fits on one line:

```r
x <- list(foo = 1, bar = 2, baz = "three")
```

but its entirely possible that I think that it is more readable in the fully expanded form. Indeed I often write list calls in the expanded form myself. Also consider pipelines like this one:

```r
df %>%
  mutate(
    col = x + y,
    col2 = y + z
  ) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

The entire `mutate()` _could_ fit on one line like this

```r
df %>%
  mutate(col = x + y, col2 = y + z) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

but many people would argue that it is more readable in fully expanded form.

This is essentially the [multi line object](https://prettier.io/docs/en/rationale#multi-line-objects) problem that prettier/biome have. Note that _there is no token in the tree that tells us that the user might want to keep it fully expanded_ (unlike in Python, where Black/ruff have magic trailing commas https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/current_style.html#labels-magic-trailing-comma). Instead, prettier/biome have a trick where they rely on the presence of _trivia_ to inform the formatting - something that is not ideal, but a decent workaround.

In particular, the rule here would be:
- If the user has an existing newline between `(` and the first token following that, 
- then force the fully expanded form, even if it would fit on one line
- otherwise use a typical `soft_line_break_or_space()` without forced expansion (i.e. expand only when you hit the line length)

The implementation for this is quite simple, for biome's JS object expressions, it is here:
https://github.com/biomejs/biome/blob/fbf4b3d3bf615915f78efd201debfa7f8dbb248b/crates/biome_js_formatter/src/utils/object_like.rs#L64-L73

Practically what this would mean is that this stays as is

```r
x <- list(
  foo = 1,
  bar = 2,
  baz = "three"
)
```

and if you want to request the flat form you can do

```r
x <- list(foo = 1,
  bar = 2,
  baz = "three"
)
```

and then save. As long as it fits on one line, it will flatten to

```r
x <- list(foo = 1, bar = 2, baz = "three")
```

and to re-request the expanded form, do this

```r
x <- list(
foo = 1, bar = 2, baz = "three")
```

and save.

For the `mutate()` example it would work the same way. It would stay expanded until you remove the line break after the `(` manually.

### Codegrip

The other reason to implement this behavior is because it would pair _very_ well with codegrip. You could continue to use codegrip to swap between flat and fully expanded forms, and because of this rule we would respect your choice.

### Drawbacks and considerations

This "feature" has a _major_ drawback - it is a "non reversible" formatting. Consider that you have dplyr code like this

```r
df %>%
  mutate(col = x + y, col2 = y + z) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

and you add a 3rd column

```r
df %>%
  mutate(col = x + y, col2 = y + z, col3 = a + really + complex + and + long_expression) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

which would auto rearrange as this because it exceeds the line limit

```r
df %>%
  mutate(
    col = x + y, 
    col2 = y + z, 
    col3 = a + really + complex + and + long_expression
  ) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

That's quite nice. But now you decide, hmm maybe that long expression is better as a function, so you do:

```r
fn <- function() {
  a + really + complex + and + long_expression
}

df %>%
  mutate(
    col = x + y, 
    col2 = y + z, 
    col3 = fn()
  ) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```

And now you are stuck with expanded form, even though the `mutate()` fits on one line! i.e. this prevents air from _reversing_ the expansion it made before, because it now thinks this is a user request. You have two options to get out of this: 1) remove the leading newline, 2) use codegrip to reflow.

In general, this is not great. It allows for:
- "style wars" to creep back in because users get a chance to debate over preferring expanded vs not expanded in cases like this.
- Erroneous git diffs from non-reversible rearrangements you may have made and then reverted

So while I do think we should implement this behavior, I think we should also consider this being one of the very few places where we add an option _that allows air to be more strict_, which seems like a good kind of option to have. Indeed, prettier is also considering this option https://github.com/prettier/prettier/pull/16163. Enabling something like `ignore-leading-newline` would have the affect that if this call _can_ be flattened, then it _will_ be flattened, bringing reversible formatting back into play (yay!).

## Line breaks between `<-` and `RHS`

Similar to the call example from above, some people really prefer a newline + tab after their `<-`. I honestly hate this 😬, but I think we could consider this being another place where leading newlines are respected unless `ignore-leading-newline` is set.

```r
df <- 
  df %>%
  mutate(
    col = x + y, 
    col2 = y + z, 
    col3 = fn()
  ) %>%
  filter(col < col2)
```
